title: Syriac
font: "Noto Sans Syriac", "Estrangelo Edessa", "Segoe UI Historic", serif
blurb: The 22 letters of the Syriac alphabet, used for Classical Syriac and the Neo-Aramaic languages, and how they join.
writeTip: These are the Estrangela shapes, the oldest of the three Syriac styles. Serto (West) and Madnhaya (East) round the same letters differently; the order and names stay the same.
notes: The Syriac alphabet for SquirrelGo Alphabets, in the Estrangela style that Noto Sans Syriac draws. Romanization follows the usual academic transliteration of Classical Syriac (ḇ ḡ ḏ ḵ p̄ ṯ for the soft sounds after a vowel); IPA gives the Classical values. Examples are common Classical Syriac nouns written without vowel points, in their emphatic (dictionary) form ending in -ā. Hints, groupings and articles are original.
Syriac has no text-to-speech voice, so sounds are recorded from the IPA.

lessons.title: ܐ to ܗ
lessons.note: Syriac is read from right to left. Like Hebrew and Arabic it writes consonants; ܐ, ܘ and ܝ also stand for long vowels.

chars.hint: ālap̄: silent, or a light catch in the throat; carries a vowel
bēṯ: b, or v after a vowel
gāmal: g as in go, or a soft gh after a vowel
dālaṯ: d, or th as in this after a vowel; the dot sits below
hē: h
waw: w, or the long vowels o and u
zayn: z
ḥēṯ: a breathy h from the throat
ṭēṯ: an emphatic t, said with the tongue pulled back
yōḏ: y as in yes, or the long vowels i and e
kāp̄: k, or ch as in Bach after a vowel
lāmaḏ: l
mīm: m
nūn: n
semkaṯ: s
ʿē: a squeeze deep in the throat, as in Arabic ʿayn
pē: p, or f after a vowel
ṣāḏē: an emphatic s, said with the tongue pulled back
qōp̄: a k from far back in the throat
rēš: a tapped r; the dot sits above
šīn: sh as in ship
taw: t, or th as in thin after a vowel

articles.title: About the Syriac alphabet
articles.body:
Syriac grew out of the Aramaic alphabet in Edessa (today's Şanlıurfa, Turkey) around the first century. It became the script of Classical Syriac, the language of a large Christian literature, and is still used for liturgy and for the modern Neo-Aramaic languages, such as Assyrian, Chaldean and Turoyo.

Syriac is written right to left, with no capital letters. Like Hebrew and Arabic it is an abjad: the 22 letters write consonants, and ܐ, ܘ and ܝ can also stand for long vowels. Vowel points, small dots or Greek-style marks above and below, are optional and mostly appear in books for learners and in liturgy.

The letters come in the same order as Hebrew's and carry the same number values: ܐ = 1, ܒ = 2, ܝ = 10.

articles.title: Joining letters
articles.body:
Syriac is joined, like Arabic: most letters connect to the letters on both sides, and their shapes change at the start, middle and end of a word.

Eight letters join only to the letter before them, never to the one after: ܐ ܕ ܗ ܘ ܙ ܨ ܪ ܬ. After one of them the next letter starts fresh, so a word can break into pieces, as in ܘܪܕܐ (wardā, rose). The letter forms table shows each letter alone, at the start, in the middle and at the end.

articles.title: Three styles
articles.body:
The same alphabet is written in three styles:

  • Estrangela, the oldest, with firm upright shapes. It is used here and for headings and older texts.
  • Serto (West Syriac), rounder and quicker, used by the Syriac Orthodox and Maronite churches and for Turoyo.
  • Madnhaya (East Syriac), used by the Assyrian and Chaldean churches and for modern Assyrian.

The letters have the same names, order and sounds in all three. Two letters that look alike in every style are ܕ (d, dot below) and ܪ (r, dot above).
